title: Bhai Bidhi Chand
hook: a former thief turned Sikh, famous in tradition for recovering the Guru's horses from Lahore in disguise

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Gurdas ran to Banaras, came back with his hands tied, and was forgiven. Your line was even he was tested. Did you let one lapse go? Today, a man whose past was worse than one lapse. Day eight hundred eleven.

Some skills don't look good on a résumé. Moving without a sound. Reading a guard's habits. Talking your way past a gate. Getting out of a place before anyone notices you're gone. Bhai Bidhi Chand had all of them, and Sikh tradition doesn't pretend otherwise: before he came to the Guru, he was a thief. What's surprising is what happened to those skills afterward. They didn't vanish. They changed owners. Today: Bhai Bidhi Chand.
screen: `SKILLS THAT DON'T LOOK GOOD ON A RÉSUMÉ.` → `HE WAS A THIEF.` → `THE SKILLS CHANGED OWNERS.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Bidhi Chand grew up in a village near Amritsar and fell in with bad company, stealing to live. Then he came into the Guru's circle, in the time of Guru Arjan, and his life turned. He became a Sikh, and later one of Guru Hargobind's trusted companions. Now the story he's known for. Tradition says devoted Sikhs from far to the west were bringing fine horses as an offering to Guru Hargobind, and on the road, officials seized them and sent them to the royal stables in Lahore Fort. Tradition names the horses Dilbagh and Gulbagh. The Guru's people were upset. And Bidhi Chand said, in effect: leave this to me. He went to Lahore dressed as a grass-cutter. He sold the stables grass so good, and so cheap, that they hired him to tend the horses. He was patient. He won the grooms' trust. And every night, the story says, he threw a heavy stone off the fort wall into the river below, so the guards grew used to the splash and stopped looking. Then one night, the splash was him. He rode the horse over the wall into the water, swam it across, and brought it to the Guru. For the second horse, tradition says, he came back in another disguise, as a fortune-teller who claimed he could find what had been stolen, and rode off with that one too. Sikhs tell this with a grin. But under the grin is something serious. The Guru didn't ask Bidhi Chand to become a different man with no past. He took the cleverness, the nerve, the patience, and turned them toward something true.
screen: `A THIEF WHO CAME TO THE GURU.` · `THE HORSES TAKEN TO LAHORE.` · `A GRASS-CUTTER AND A NIGHTLY SPLASH.` · `OVER THE WALL, INTO THE RIVER.` · then, large: `A THIEF TURNED TRUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: use a clever skill for good. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Then ask yourself, honestly: what's a skill I have that I'm a little embarrassed by? Talking people round. Finding loopholes. Noticing what others miss. Getting things done fast and not quite by the book. Don't judge it. Just name it. Then picture one way that same skill could help someone today: getting a neighbor's problem solved, untangling a form for someone, spotting what a friend needs. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bidhi Chand. A former thief who became a Sikh and, tradition says, brought the Guru's horses back from Lahore in disguise. Today's word.
Your line: a thief turned true. Today, put the skill you named in the sit to work for someone else, once, and notice how it feels to use it in the open. Day eight hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Bhai Bidhi Chand as one of the companions of Guru Hargobind, remembered for his courage and cleverness after he left a life of theft and came to the Guru.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Bhai Bidhi Chand; Bhai, brother, is a title of respect.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fun heist story.
what it means: a former thief whose cleverness and nerve, tradition says, were turned to the Guru's service.
what a scholar hears: the story belongs to the time of Guru Hargobind, when Sikh tradition remembers the Guru's household keeping horses and arms.

notes: Bidhi Chand's village (Sur Singh, near Amritsar) and his earlier life of theft: from the common telling; confirm.
The horses' origin ('from far to the west', often said to be from Kabul) and the names Dilbagh and Gulbagh: tradition; confirm.
The grass-cutter disguise, the nightly stone, the leap into the Ravi and the fortune-teller disguise follow the common telling; details vary.
'Sikhs tell this with a grin' is a tone description; a Keeper may want it softened.
Gurmukhi spelling ਭਾਈ ਬਿਧੀ ਚੰਦ: confirm.
